items.title: Caribische bibliotheken versterken samenwerking tijdens uitwisselingsweek in El Salvador
items.raw_text: Hoe bouw je samen aan een sterk netwerk van bibliotheken, terwijl je ook over grenzen heen van elkaar blijft leren? Die vraag stond centraal tijdens een bijzondere uitwisselingsweek in El Salvador. Bibliotheken uit het Caribisch deel van ons Koninkrijk kwamen samen om kennis en ervaringen met elkaar te delen en om een belangrijke stap te zetten in hun gezamenlijke ontwikkeling. Tijdens de conferentie ondertekenden Biblioteka Nashonal Kòrsou , Biblioteca Nacional Aruba , Biblioteka Públiko Boneiru , Sint Maarten Library , Gertrude Judson Bicentennial Public Library St. Eustatius en Queen Wilhelmina Library hun gezamenlijke netwerkplan. Daarmee bekrachtigen zij hun gedeelde ambities en afspraken voor de komende periode. Een netwerk met ambitie De Caribische bibliotheken werken, met begeleiding van Common Eye , aan een sterk en duurzaam netwerk dat aansluit bij hun eigen behoeften, ervaringen en ambities. Het netwerkplan richt zich onder andere op een sterkere positionering van de Caribische bibliotheken en de ontwikkeling van toekomstbestendige bibliotheken. Als kennis- en expertisepartner zijn wij vanuit Rijnbrink, samen met de Koninklijke Bibliotheek (KB) , betrokken bij het netwerk. items.title: Hoe de VoorleesExpress gezinnen versterkt en bibliotheken scherper laat werken

items.title: Prentenboeken in Papiamentu: een feest van herkenning
items.raw_text: Een prentenboek vertalen lijkt eenvoudig: je zet de ene taal om in de andere. Maar hoe zorg je ervoor dat een kind zich écht herkent in een verhaal? Voor de nieuwe Papiamentu-prentenboeken – gerealiseerd in het project Leesbevordering in meertalige gezinnen – dachten leden van de klankbordgroep mee over taal, cultuur en geschiedenis. Waarom is de keuze voor opa beter dan de officiële vertaling tawela? Waarom mocht het verhaal van Tula in de nieuwe prentenboekencollectie niet ontbreken? En wat gebeurt er als een kind voor het eerst een verhaal in zijn eigen taal hoort? Jakeema, Myrthe en Margriet vertellen hoe juist die keuzes het verschil maken. Waarom vertalen nodig was Zoals het eerdere artikel over dit project al aangaf: voorlezen stimuleert de taalontwikkeling van jonge kinderen het beste. Juist voorlezen in de thuistaal, de taal van het hart, levert veel extra’s op. Ouders op Bonaire willen dat met alle liefde doen, vertelt Jakeema Hernandez, programmaleider bij Bibliotheek Bonaire. Maar de collectie prentenboeken in het Papiamentu is beperkt. Jakeema is dan ook blij met de nieuwe, vertaalde Papiamentu-boeken. Als kind hield ik al van lezen, maar een boek in mijn eigen taal vinden in de boekhandel of bibliotheek was onmogelijk. Voor mijn inner child is het mooi om te zien dat er nu boeken in het Papiamentu bestaan. items.title: Voorlezen in de taal van je hart: meer verhalen in Farsi en Papiamentu
items.raw_text: Een Curaçaos meisje dat glundert als ze het boek ‘Mihó nò’ ontdekt tussen de bibliotheekboeken. Een Iranese vader die een bibliotheekmedewerker speciaal komt bedanken, omdat hij een prentenboek in zijn thuistaal mee kan nemen. Of een Farsi-sprekende moeder die ontroerd raakt, als ze tijdens een bijeenkomst hoort dat dromen en schelden in je thuistaal normaal is. Deze voorbeelden vertellen wat waardering voor thuistalen met mensen doet. Het geeft het gevoel dat jij ertoe doet, dat je verhaal welkom is en dat je je thuis mag voelen. Die kunnen bibliotheken sinds half juli bestellen en combineren met meertalige voorleesfilmpjes via de Jeugdbibliotheek en De Voorleeshoek. Ouders en kinderen die samen lezen, luisteren en praten in de taal van hun hart: dáár gaan wij van glunderen! De viering van de Farsi en Papiamentu voorleesfilmpjes met de projectpartners en leesmediaconsulenten uit Bonaire. Praten en voorlezen in de thuistaal? Doen! Voorlezen stimuleert de taalontwikkeling van jonge kinderen het beste. Kinderen die opgroeien in een rijke taalomgeving, ontwikkelen een grotere woordenschat en meer plezier in taal. items.raw_text: ECP-directeur Arie van Bellen ging in een recente aflevering van de podcastreeks ECP Talks in gesprek met ECP-programmaregisseur Sabine Herbrink over het programma Digitaal Doordacht. Zij bespraken hoe het programma de overheid helpt om bewuste, doordachte keuzes te maken in onze snel digitaliserende samenleving. Het gesprek ging niet alleen over de kansen zoals dwarsverbanden tussen thema’s en de meerwaarde die het programma biedt in de digitalisering van de overheid, maar ook over de uitdagingen rondom verantwoorde inzet, innovatie en samenwerking. items.title: Van regisserende naar ontwerpende overheid

In de gesprekken met Marc Minnee en Marco de Bruijn van het ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken en Koninkrijksrelaties (BZK) staat centraal waar verandering daadwerkelijk ontstaat: wanneer professionals elkaar vinden, aannames bespreekbaar maken en keuzes maken die bijdragen aan versnelling én duurzame borging. Zo laten de verhalen zien hoe digitalisering door concrete interventies kan bijdragen aan een toekomstgerichte overheid waarin burgers en ondernemers centraal staan, met blijvende aandacht voor ethiek, privacy, security en maatschappelijk vertrouwen. Op 24 juni vond in Amare voor de vijfde keer de CIO-dag plaats. Voor een zaal vol CIO’s schetsten Marc Minnee, innovatiemanager voor het ministerie van BZK, en Marco de Bruijn, beleidsmedewerker AI bij het ministerie van BZK, hun NDS AI-visie op de inzet van generatieve AI-modellen bij de overheid. Hun verhaal begint bij taalmodellen, maar raakt al snel aan een veel fundamentelere vraag: hoe houdt de overheid zelf regie over haar digitale toekomst? Binnen de Nederlandse Digitaliseringsstrategie is AI daarom een prioriteit: de overheid wil AI verantwoord inzetten voor maatschappelijke opgaven en betere dienstverlening, succesvolle toepassin

items.title: OTC Whitepaper Soevereiniteit
items.raw_text: Digitale soevereiniteit betekent niet dat organisaties alle digitale diensten zelf moeten bezitten of beheren. Het betekent dat zij aantoonbare grip hebben op kritieke digitale afhankelijkheden: inzicht in de keten, bewuste risicoacceptatie, uitvoerbare alternatieven, onafhankelijke controle en transparante communicatie over keuzes en restrisico’s. In het whitepaper over digitale soevereiniteit vertaalt de Online Trust Coalitie dit thema naar een praktisch handelingskader voor bestuurders, IT-verantwoordelijken, toezichthouders, serviceproviders en risk- en compliancefuncties. De OTC stelt dat digitale soevereiniteit niet draait om volledige autonomie of autarkie, maar om aantoonbare beheersing: inzicht in kritieke digitale afhankelijkheden, expliciete risicoafweging, uitvoerbare exit-mogelijkheden, onafhankelijke controle en heldere communicatie over restrisico’s en gemaakte keuzes. De OTC signaleert dat impliciet vertrouwen in digitale diensten onder druk staat. Geopolitieke spanningen, conflicterende rechtsstelsels, concentratie van leveranciersmacht en complexe beheerketens maken zichtbaar dat organisaties niet langer kunnen volstaan met contracten, certificaten of algemene toezeggingen. items.title: ‘Veranderen doe je via consensus én met fermheid’
items.raw_text: Binnen Digitaal Doordacht onderzoeken we hoe digitalisering in de publieke sector daadwerkelijk bijdraagt aan betere dienstverlening, meer openheid en groter vertrouwen. Het veranderverhaal van Jolein Baidenmann laat zien dat echte openheid niet draait om simpelweg méér informatie openbaar maken, maar om informatie die voor mensen daadwerkelijk begrijpelijk en bruikbaar is. Wat haar aanpak bijzonder maakt, is hoe zij in een complexe publieke omgeving beweging creëert: door belangen zichtbaar te maken, partijen te verbinden en draagvlak te combineren met duidelijke keuzes. “Soms moet je als leider keuzes maken en stevig zijn: ik heb iedereen gehoord, maar we gaan toch die kant op.” Jolein Baidenmann is verandermanager en werkt met die insteek aan een overheid die openheid op een betekenisvolle manier probeert waar te maken. “Het is belangrijk dat een open overheid de samenleving in staat stelt om mee te denken, te controleren en gebruik te maken van de informatie die bij de overheid beschikbaar is.” Als manager Open Overheid en plaatsvervangend directeur Open Overheid bij het ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken en Koninkrijksrelaties (BZK) is Baidenmann bij uitstek de persoon om het concept ‘open overheid’ in praktijk te brengen. items.title: Juli
items.raw_text: Online radicalisering van jongeren: het gesprek gaat door Deze maand is er opnieuw veel aandacht voor schadelijke en gewelddadige online netwerken. De NOS berichtte op 23 juli over de aanhouding van een jonge man die wordt verdacht van deelname aan een sadistisch Com-netwerk ofwel community. Binnen dergelijke besloten online groepen kunnen kwetsbare jongeren worden geronseld en aangezet tot zelfbeschadiging, misbruik en geweld. De actuele berichtgeving raakt direct aan de onderwerpen die op 22 juni centraal stonden tijdens het symposium Online radicalisering van jongeren: herkennen, begrijpen en handelen, georganiseerd door de ATKM, de NCTV en ECP. Onder leiding van dagvoorzitter Liesbeth Rasker gingen professionals, onderzoekers en ervaringsdeskundigen in gesprek over de vraag hoe online radicalisering tijdig kan worden herkend, zonder jongeren te snel te veroordelen of te stigmatiseren. Radicalisering begint vaak niet met een uitgesproken ideologie of een duidelijke intentie om geweld te gebruiken. Het kan beginnen bij menselijke vragen: wie ben ik, waar hoor ik bij en wie neemt mij serieus? Online groepen kunnen daarop inspelen en grenzen tussen humor, provocatie, uitsluiting en geweld geleidelijk laten vervagen. De rode draad in het symposium, de podcast en de actuele berichtgeving is daarom dezelfde: blijf nieuwsgierig, investeer in kennis van de online leefwereld en voer het gesprek voordat standpunten en gedrag verder verharden. items.title: Zomerblog Marjolijn Bonthuis
items.raw_text: “Worden we een museum?” Een persoonlijke zomerse beschouwing over Europa, AI en de stap van dialoog naar daadkracht Deze zomer lees ik Grand Hotel Europa van Ilja Leonard Pfeijffer. Het hotel in de roman staat symbool voor Europa: prachtig, rijk aan verhalen, maar vooral gericht op het verleden. Europa bewaart zijn kunst, architectuur en geschiedenis — en verkoopt die aan toeristen. Ondertussen wordt de toekomst elders gebouwd. Die gedachte dringt zich ook op wanneer ik kijk naar de huidige technologische ontwikkelingen. Terwijl Amerikaanse en Chinese bedrijven miljarden investeren in kunstmatige intelligentie, chips en digitale infrastructuur, zijn wij in Europa vaak vooral bezig met regels, risico’s en bescherming. Laat ik daar duidelijk over zijn: die aandacht is nodig. Zeker vanuit mijn dagelijkse verantwoordelijkheid voor digitale veiligheid, weerbaarheid en vertrouwen weet ik hoe belangrijk het is dat technologie niet zonder grenzen wordt ontwikkeld en toegepast. Big Tech heeft inmiddels zoveel economische, technologische en maatschappelijke macht opgebouwd dat stevige publieke kaders onvermijdelijk zijn. Bescherming van grondrechten, democratische controle en eerlijke concurrentie zijn geen luxe. Maar regels alleen maken ons nog geen speler. Als Europa vooral vastlegt onder welke voorwaarden technologie van anderen hier mag worden gebruikt, terwijl we zelf onvoldoende investeren in de ontwikkeling ervan, blijft onze invloed beperkt. items.title: IFLA turns 99: The countdown begins!
items.raw_text: Today IFLA celebrates its 99th birthday. Some might say that only big, round number anniversaries should be celebrated, but we haven’t made it this far by following the crowd. So, let us be defiant of expectations, and make today also an opportunity to celebrate, looking back to what we have achieved, but also looking forward to what awaits us in 2027 and well beyond. What is IFLA now, almost a century after its creation? A global community made of over 1600 members and more than 1000 active, passionate volunteers working hard to change the library field for the better. A place where we celebrate the past but look at technology, knowledge and innovation with optimism in order to achieve sustainable futures for all. An organisation that has always striven to make the world a better place. Libraries make our lives better and IFLA supports libraries globally through its international advocacy, professional standards, capacity building, and resource sharing. We have got this far because our core mission and values are lasting, giving us a key reference point and source of resilience in times of change. Today, like so many times in the past, we and the societies are being shaped and reshaped by dramatic political, economic, environmental, and social trends. Access to appropriate devices and services, digital and AI literacy, and trusted assistance in navigating AI-enabled information and public-service environments are all critical for bridging the digital divide. Claire McGuire (IFLA), Radka Sibille (UPU), Nick Buron (Queens Public Library/ALA), and Kevin Hernandez (UPU). This Digital@UNGA Affiliate Session, co-organised by the Universal Postal Union and IFLA, explored why public access institutions like libraries, schools and post offices are critical connectivity infrastructure, and how existing funding mechanisms could be better deployed to support meaningful access for all. items.title: AVMS at WLIC 2026 in Busan: accessible audiovisual libraries and multimedia innovation
items.raw_text: At the 2026 IFLA World Library and Information Congress (WLIC) in Busan, Korea, the IFLA Audiovisual and Multimedia Section (AVMS) organized two open sessions that addressed key developments in audiovisual librarianship, accessibility, and multimedia innovation. Accessible Audiovisual Libraries: Standards, Workflows, and Inclusive Discovery in the Age of Streaming The first session officially presented the revised IFLA Guidelines for Audiovisual Resources in Libraries and Other Institutions (2026). The guidelines respond to major shifts in the audiovisual landscape, including streaming services, accessibility requirements, audiovisual literacy, and the emergence of AI in library services. After an overview of the guidelines’ structure, invited speakers explored inclusive workflows, metadata and discovery, accessible streaming, AI for accessibility, and service evaluation. Visualizing Art: Multimedia Transformations in Libraries The second session , jointly organized with the Art Libraries Section, examined the role of multimedia technologies in the transformation of art libraries and cultural heritage institutions. It opened with a keynote on multimedia integration in art library architecture, followed by live demonstrations of innovative projects and tools, with an interactive audience vote for the most innovative contribution. items.title: IFLA endorses International Science Council definition of the Right to Science
items.raw_text: Despite appearing in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the right to science – both to participate in and benefit from science – too often does not enjoy the same profile as other rights. Yet the costs of failing to uphold this are significant, not just in terms of academics’ own ability to pursue their work free from undue pressures from governments and others, but also in the quality, accessibility and usability of research outputs by the wider population. Politically motivated cuts, bans on addressing certain topics, the withdrawal of access to key resources, the blocking or defunding of international cooperation, the incompleteness of the drive towards open access, and underinvestment in citizen science and science communication – all put into question the right to science. In order to consolidate efforts by the community in order to resist these trends, and promote this right as both a goal in itself and an enabler of so many other goals, the International Science Council (of which IFLA is a member and partner) has developed a definition of the Right to Science . This expands on what is present in the Universal Declaration, but remains accessible. It condenses down much existing work, including at the UN Human Rights Council as well, as well as taking account of the need also for responsibility in science, not least in implementing the CARE principles when working with Indigenous communities. items.title: Coding schemes and context: making qualitative research credible
items.raw_text: A conversation about what makes qualitative research credible Champaign-Urbana, Illinois, United States – On September 22nd, 2026, Jess Hagman, the Social Sciences Research Librarian at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, led a discussion on qualitative research quality during the webinar Negotiating Qualitative Research Quality in the Age of AI, co-hosted by the Science and Technology Libraires Section and the Social Science Libraries Section . The webinar explored how researchers can think beyond individual technical tools and consider the broader methodological context surrounding qualitative analysis. It also examined qualitative research across disciplines, including education, social sciences, engineering and health sciences, with particular attention to the challenges researchers face when deciding how to analyze qualitative data. Hagman emphasized that qualitative research has “too many meanings,” offering researchers considerable freedom but also requiring them to explain and justify the choices they make. Rather than treating analysis as a sequence of technical steps, she described it as a process intended to make claims about data that can then be used to answer a research question. Methodology, assumptions, and audiences A central theme of the webinar was methodological congruence: the methods used to collect, analyze and present data should make sense together and align with the assumptions underlying a study. items.title: Call for Papers – Getting Engaged with Library Associations
items.raw_text: Call for Papers The Webinar Series for LIS Students aims to create a space for Library and Information Science (LIS) students to share their research, projects, and ideas on current and emerging topics in librarianship and information science. Each webinar addresses a specific theme. All events are held online and are open to everyone (no registration fees). The series is a project by IFLA Division C and the Section on Education and Training. Webinar Theme Five Years Later: Getting Engaged with Library Associations – What Has Changed? This webinar is a follow-up to the webinar “Getting Engaged with Library Associations – Benefits, Issues, Factors”, held on 22 April 2021. Five years later, this webinar provides an opportunity to reflect on what has changed in the relationship between early-career librarians, LIS students and professional associations. The webinar will explore how motivations and barriers to engagement have developed over the past five years, how today’s early-career librarians view professional associations and what opportunities exist for getting involved in library associations, including IFLA. A key goal of this webinar is to encourage LIS students to engage with professional associations, to explore the benefits and opportunities that such engagement can offer and to discuss how library associations can become more attractive and accessible to the next generation of library and information professionals. items.title: IFLA Futures Club #5: Erik Boekesteijn and Cathelijne Kuiters
items.raw_text: We’re looking forward to sharing some real-world practitioner perspectives on how to apply futures thinking within the library context with the next edition of IFLA’s Futures Club: 6 October, 13:30-15:00 UTC ( see what time this is for you ). The Club is intended as a space for informal conversation and learning about how we can integrate futures into the planning and work of libraries around the world. With a combination of key thinkers on relevant issues as well as people making them a reality on the ground, it aims to provide a form of introduction to futures thinking. Following our conversation with Brewster Kahle, founder of the Internet Archive, we’re returning to Europe for our fifth episode, where Erik Boekesteijn and Cathelijne Kuiters of the National Library of the Netherlands (KB) to share their experience of launching a futures initiative within the KB and across the wider Dutch library field. The KB has embraced future thinking, looking to draw on it both as a means of engaging staff across the institution in reflection on future strategy, but also in its outreach to the public. In this context, Erik and Cathelijne have led an impressive portfolio of initiatives that have not only demonstrated the benefits of futures thinking, but also revealed helpful lessons about what works – and what doesn’t – in doing so. items.title: IFLA Futures Club #4: Brewster Kahle: “Dive In”
items.raw_text: The fourth edition of our Futures Club welcomed a guest who has had a huge impact on the shape of our current information environment, the founder of the Internet Archive, Brewster Kahle. With a focus on promoting the discoverability of information for over 40 years – well before the invention of the World Wide Web – he has a unique experience and insight into the forces shaping the internet, and where it is going next. What we expect and what we get Looking back at the future expected back in the 80s and 90s, key was the idea that the shift in format from physical to digital created opportunities to do things differently, and better. The goal became to make the Library of Congress available to anyone at their desktops, overcoming all of the barriers created by distance and more. The irony was that despite this goal, remote access to the full collections of libraries never happened. Nor did the Encyclopedia Britannica make its way online, but rather had to be built again – with much lower copyright barriers – in the form of Wikipedia. Various forces may have been behind this – a failure to anticipate that people would look to their screens for answers, not just entertainment for one. There had been conservatism on all sides, and particularly around the exploitation of copyright. The potential of the internet to allow right-holders unprecedented levels of control over access to and use of content has led to platforms and publishers trying to do libraries’ job. items.title: Refreshing for the Future
items.raw_text: Library renovations can feel overwhelming—especially when you’re juggling tight budgets, big community expectations, and a building that’s showing its age. The good news is you don’t have to choose between “do nothing” and “tear it down.” Most successful library upgrades live somewhere in the middle: a smart, phased plan that protects your long-term vision while making meaningful improvements right now. Here are a few practical ways to think about approaching a library renovation: Start with a North Star. Before you pick finishes or start talking timelines, take a step back and get clarity on what you want your library to become. I call this the north star —your vision for how the building should function for staff and the public. Even if you only have funding for part of the work today, guiding principles help you avoid spending money on changes you’ll undo later. Renovations are much easier when everyone can point to the same end goal—even if you’re getting there in phases. Assess the building first. It’s tempting to jump straight into visible improvements, but understanding existing conditions is what sets a project up for success. A solid facility-condition evaluation looks at the status of major building systems and flags components that may be nearing the end of their life cycle, such as mechanical systems, electrical panel capacity, and even finishes like carpet. items.title: Limiting Risk in the Face of Uncertainty
items.raw_text: If you save for retirement when you are young, the standard advice is to emphasize stock-based exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds. Stocks increase and decrease in dramatic ways that no one can predict reliably, so this approach carries some risk. Fortunately for US stock market investors, that risk has historically been rewarded, on average and over the long term, with high returns. As you approach retirement and need to rely on investments to cover living expenses, the standard advice is to shift your portfolio toward bond-based ETFs or mutual funds. Bonds have had fewer and less dramatic booms and busts. For this reason, they are generally considered less risky than stocks. On average, over the long term, bonds’ safety has meant lower, more reliable returns than stocks. Risk makes less sense for ALA right now. Because of its financial deficit , the Association needs stability. Therefore, in April, ALA’s Endowment Trustees updated the target allocation for the Association’s investment portfolio, reducing our holdings of stocks from 50% to 40%, and increasing ALA’s holdings of bonds from 30% to 40%. As a result, we are sacrificing some projected returns to limit projected risk. If stocks boom as they have in the past few years, ALA’s portfolio will not increase as much as it would have. items.raw_text: Welcome to American Libraries’ 2026 Library Design Showcase, our annual celebration of new and renovated libraries across the US and Canada. The word welcome appeared in many of this year’s submissions, reflecting a growing understanding that in anxious times, the library is a place that should feel good: safe, comfortable, well-lit, plugged in, and deeply connected to its surroundings. More than two-thirds of this year’s 15 selections are renovations or adaptive reuse projects. Libraries of all types are finding ways to acknowledge historical and environmental realities, embrace natural elements and cultural identities, evolve traditions, and build in flexibility to account for the unexpected. Read on for snapshots of these communities in motion. Natural immersion Maplewood (N.J.) Memorial Library Adjacent to a historic park, with protected natural areas on all sides, this 1955 masonry structure had nowhere to expand but up. The new, light-filled second floor features bird-safe glass, wood battens, and green roofs for a treehouse feel. The all-electric building, the first LEED Gold–certified library in New Jersey, includes solar panels that offset more than half of the library’s energy use. items.title: Secrets of Effective Upskilling
items.raw_text: This is an excerpt from Upskilling for Library Workers: A Guide for Future-Ready Professionals by Ann Medaille (ALA Editions, 2026). With the advent of new technologies and rapid social and economic shifts, library workers’ jobs are being transformed. Compared with a decade ago, library workers now spend more time consulting on complex research tools, teaching digital literacy classes, supporting virtual learning environments, helping users troubleshoot devices, and codesigning projects with community partners. The pace at which library staffers are called upon to learn new skills is accelerating, and workers may struggle to keep up. In addition, automation and artificial intelligence (AI) are altering many aspects of work. In the long run, technological innovations have the potential to increase productivity and lead to more interesting kinds of work, but in the short term, they often cause disruptions that can be difficult for workers to navigate. To address these changes—and manage the anxieties that come along with them—workers need constant support for skill development. While corporations may embrace upskilling to stay competitive, libraries will have to support upskilling to remain relevant. Library leaders are under greater pressure to respond rapidly to changing social and economic conditions and demonstrate that their libraries make a difference in their communities. items.title: Hold the Phone
items.raw_text: Since fall 2024, each school day at Grant High School in Portland, Oregon, has started the same way: Roughly 2,100 students line up to place their phones in gray and green Yondr pouches—the kind live performers use to prevent audience members from recording—as they enter the building. From the morning bell to dismissal, phones are sealed and can be unlocked only with special magnets near the school’s exits as students leave for the day. The high school’s effort to limit phone use on campus has received support from its educators, who say classroom engagement is on the rise, and mixed reviews from students, who dislike being cut off from their devices. But there’s been one unexpected outcome of the policy: More students are spending time in the library, where they’re browsing the collection or hanging out during free periods, says teacher-librarian Paige Battle. “They’re checking out more books, and I feel like that’s been so important in their education,” Battle says. “We’re seeing studies about students, even adults, not having the reading stamina they’ve had in the past, so I’ve been encouraged by this increase.” Roughly six in 10 parents of an 11- or 12-year-old say their child owns a smartphone, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey . And as more schools across the country enact phone-free policies—29 states and the District of Columbia have instituted bell-to-bell phone-free policies so far—many school libraries are experiencing a surge in popularity. items.title: Newsmaker: Min Jin Lee
items.raw_text: Min Jin Lee has notched career milestones that few authors reach. Her immigration saga Pachinko was both a National Book Award finalist and a New York Times Top 10 Best Book of 2017, and it was adapted into a television series of the same name for Apple TV. Lee is also a Guggenheim fellow and the first Korean American to hold the role of New York State author laureate. Her latest title, American Hagwon (Cardinal, September), examines the influence of Korean “cram schools” among families in the Korean diaspora. American Libraries spoke with Lee ahead of her appearance at the American Library Association’s 2026 Annual Conference and Exhibition in Chicago. She discussed her new book, the library that shaped her, and her antidote to book bans. What inspired you to focus on the education system as it relates to the movements of a middle-class Korean American family in American Hagwon ? My research process involved all these interviews—I’ve done hundreds of them, probably almost 1,000 at this point—and every single time I talked to somebody, they would mention their education path. It was such an important and controversial subject. I thought, if I had to think about the most important value for Koreans, especially in the diaspora, what would I write about? Education turned out to be a beast, because people have lots of feelings about it. In the book, the Koh family loses wealth and status as they weather betrayal and financial crises. items.title: Mall Wonder
items.raw_text: After serving its community for nearly 45 years in the same building, Escondido (Calif.) Public Library closed in April 2025 for an $11.6 million renovation. It was important to us, as the city’s lone library, to preserve access during construction. So one month later, our library opened a temporary location in a very different kind of facility: the nearby North County Mall, where services and collections were spread across six storefronts, including a former Abercrombie & Fitch clothing store. Of course, moving a library takes more than a month. Our planning took more than a year and required staff to work under tight deadlines, limited budgets, and high expectations. Here’s how we did it, and what we learned from the process. Choosing a location. It’s essential to consider whether the new location will match, improve upon, or limit access. Retailers and mall operators have already studied traffic patterns, visibility, parking, and nearby amenities. Leverage that knowledge to evaluate access. In our case, the public benefited from a highway and bus stop near the mall, and adjacency to a city park. The arrangement also gave the mall a stable civic tenant and created natural cross-traffic between library patrons and shoppers. The mall was not just available space; it was a location where public access, economic development, and community visibility could overlap. items.title: Dismantling Disinformation
items.raw_text: Library workers are well aware of the effects of book bans and censorship. Propaganda and disinformation are the flipside of the same coin. Understanding the complex relationships among these interrelated processes is more critical than ever, especially as libraries explore possible solutions and responses. The following books show how disinformation can lead to censorship and how censorship can, in turn, allow disinformation to thrive. Book Bans, Disinformation, and Cultural Erasure: The Censor­ship Movement in Libraries, Schools, and Society By Paul T. Jaeger Jaeger situates the current book-banning movement within a larger social and political effort to erase marginalized communities and culture. He provides clear definitions and examples of these processes and goals, including the roles played by technological progress and economic inequity. With accessible references (like the Beatles, Dungeons & Dragons, and Holmes and Watson) and nuanced examinations of McCarthyism, the history of libraries, and the myth of neutrality, this is a recommended read for anyone interested in a more expansive understanding of current First Amendment challenges. items.title: Book Industry Study Group (BISG) and BookNet Canada Release 2026 Report on AI Use Across the North American Book Industry
items.raw_text: From a Joint Release: The Book Industry Study Group (BISG) and BookNet Canada have released AI Use Across the North American Book Industry 2026 , the second annual report examining how publishing professionals and organizations across the U.S. and Canada are using—and thinking about—AI. Drawing on 771 responses, this year’s report provides an opportunity to look beyond a single snapshot and begin tracking how AI adoption, attitudes, policies, and concerns are changing over time. [Clip] An Industry Moving Toward More Structured AI Use One of the clearest changes from 2025 is happening at the organizational level. In 2026, 63% of respondents said their organization is using AI, up from 48% in 2025. Individual use moved in the opposite direction, falling from 46% to 38%. Organization size also matters: 88% of organizations with more than 100 employees reported using AI. Adoption does not necessarily mean unrestricted use. The most common organizational approach is to encourage AI within controlled workflows or for specific tasks, while 49% of respondents said their organization now has an official AI policy or guidelines, up from 31% in 2025. [Clip] Concerns Remain High Greater organizational adoption has not diminished concerns about AI. Copyright remains a leading issue, cited by 86% of respondents. items.title: Report: Oxford Lets OpenAI Train Its AI Models On Historical Texts From the Bodleian Library
items.raw_text: From The Guardian: The University of Oxford has allowed the company behind ChatGPT to train its AI models on historical texts from its Bodleian Library, as tech companies scour academic institutions for fresh data. The Bodleian material digitised by OpenAI has been used to “populate the OpenAI training set”, according to internal documents. Oxford announced a partnership with the company in March 2025, using OpenAI software to digitise texts from the university’s world-famous library, which it said would make the content more widely available for students and researchers. However, the announcement did not state the material would be used for training OpenAI’s models, which are trained to recognise patterns in words – and thus “learn” to write complete sentences and perform other cognitive tasks – by being fed vast amounts of data. [Clip] Meeting minutes at the University of Oxford, obtained via a freedom of information request, record concerns from staff, including members of the Bodleian governance committee, about the reputational risk of partnering with OpenAI and the effect on the university’s environmental commitments of striking a deal involving an energy-intensive technology. items.title: National Science Foundation (NSF) Announces Launch of the Open Knowledge Network, A National Open-Data Platform Connecting More Than 40 Knowledge Graphs
items.raw_text: From an NSF Announcement: Built through the NSF Prototype Open Knowledge Network program and in collaboration with a broad coalition of federal partners, the network is now available for public use The U.S. National Science Foundation announced today the launch of the NSF Open Knowledge Network (NSF OKN), a national open-data infrastructure that links 43 interconnected knowledge graphs and tens of billions of connected facts across health, the environment, justice, manufacturing, and national security. The network is live and open to the public at okn.us . NSF OKN provides a structured, persistent, verifiable knowledge layer to complement contemporary artificial intelligence models, providing grounding of facts, attribution, and knowledge governance essential to critical AI applications in a number of fields. OKN’s value goes beyond machines querying structured knowledge: Its deeper value provides AI systems with a shared, explicit, interoperable, and auditable representation of the world on which they are expected to reason and act. Across science, government, and many key enterprise applications, valuable datasets sit in silos that are not accessible, interoperable, nor ready for use by AI systems. OKN makes federal and public data findable, connected, and machine-readable at a national scale. items.raw_text: For more than thirty years I have been interested in one deceptively simple question: How do we find things? At first glance, the answer appears obvious. We search. But anyone who has spent a lifetime in libraries knows that searching and finding are not the same thing. Throughout my earlier articles in Public Libraries Online , I explored several aspects of this process. In Finding Answers , I argued that patrons rarely come looking for information; they come looking for answers. In Search vs. Research , I suggested that locating information is only the beginning of inquiry. In Keeping Things Found , I examined what happens after discovery, how knowledge is preserved, organized, and made retrievable for future use. Artificial intelligence is now transforming how people search and, perhaps more importantly, how they find. For the first time in history, millions of people no longer begin by opening a directory, consulting an index, or scanning pages of search results. Instead, they ask a question in ordinary language and receive what appears to be a finished answer. This is more than another improvement in search technology. items.title: How Library Science Principles Power Community AI Literacy
items.raw_text: Public libraries are dealing with budget cuts, book bans, and the usual existential questions about whether anyone needs physical collections when they can google everything. And now AI shows up, and everyone assumes libraries are about to get steamrolled by it too. But watch what’s happening at reference desks across the country. Patrons ask how to determine whether an IRS email is real or a phishing attempt generated by AI. Small business owners are trying to figure out which AI tool won’t steal their marketing copy. Retired community members want to use AI to parse dense municipal documents but do not know where to start. A parent is concerned about their teenager using AI for homework and whether that’s cheating. These aren’t edge cases. This is what reference work looks like now. Much has been written about how libraries can use AI tools internally—chatbots for reference, algorithms for cataloging, and predictive analytics for collection development. But there’s another question we need to answer: How do libraries help communities navigate AI? And here’s what I realized while building AI governance frameworks: these are not computer science problems. They’re library science problems—questions about provenance, access, evaluation, and trust. The exact questions libraries have been answering for over a century, just dressed up in a new syntax. items.title: Tag! You’re It: RFID’s Big Play in Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology has become one of the most influential innovations shaping the future of library operations. Since its introduction into library settings in the late 1990s, RFID has steadily evolved from an experimental enhancement to a widely adopted tool for improving circulation, inventory management, and patron experience. As libraries continue to modernize and adapt to changing user expectations, understanding RFID, including its capabilities, limitations, and long-term implications, is essential for informed decision-making. This article provides a thorough overview of RFID technology in libraries, synthesizing research, case studies, and industry standards to help public librarians evaluate whether RFID is the right investment for their institutions. Understanding RFID Technology in Libraries RFID tags come in two primary forms: active and passive. Libraries exclusively use passive tags, which do not require an internal power source and are small enough to be concealed within books and media cases. Passive tags contain information that is picked up by a scanner, while active tags emit their own signals. In library settings, RFID tags store essential item information like title, author, call number, and location and can be read without direct line-of-sight. It had been 12 years since I last attended PLA, and I had forgotten just how exciting and energizing it can be to gather with library workers from across the country. I returned home reinvigorated, renewed, and more excited than ever to be part of our increasingly important community of librarians and information professionals. The morning keynote sessions featuring Bryan Stevenson and Dr. Ruha Benjamin were especially galvanizing. Stevenson shared how his grandmother changed his life by nurturing his love of reading, opening doors that a young boy from Alabama could scarcely have imagined. I am still reflecting on Dr. Benjamin’s perspective on AI, which she reframed, in part, as Ancestral Intelligence rather than Artificial Intelligence. The closing session with Lakota chef Sean Sherman felt especially meaningful as my library prepares to host the Americans traveling exhibit. items.title: “I Wanted To Write Something That Felt More Like A Hug” – DeAndra Davis On Her Enchanting Coming-Of-Age Novel
items.raw_text: Despite being smart, funny, and her class’s valedictorian, Jaliya has spent much of her high school career ignored by her classmates. After graduation, her dad encourages her to leave their South Florida home to spend the summer in Jamaica with her family, who she hasn’t seen in several years. Although reluctant to do so, Jaliya changes her mind after receiving an unsigned letter postmarked from Jamaica asking when she’s going to return there. Convinced the letter is from her estranged mother, Jaliya devises a plan to return to Jamaica, find her mother, and figure out once and for all why she left their family long ago. Yet once she’s back in Jamaica, Jaliya’s life grows unexpectedly richer. She reconnects with childhood friends and finds herself caught in a love triangle between her schoolgirl crush, Andre, and an intriguing new girl, India, who has just moved to her cousin’s neighborhood. items.title: Expanding Access Through Inclusive Collections
items.raw_text: Receiving a scholarship to attend PLA 2026 in Minneapolis gave me the opportunity to learn from innovative libraries and inspiring information professionals. One session in particular, “Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities,” presented by Plano Public Library and Libraries for All LLC, reinforced a simple but urgent idea: if members of our community cannot meaningfully use our materials, we are not fully meeting our mission. Access is about more than having a collection. It is about ensuring that everyone can engage with and benefit from it. The session highlighted how people with disabilities are often underserved by traditional library collections. While many libraries offer large print, braille, and other accessible formats, these resources do not address the full range of patron needs. Some readers may have physical disabilities that make turning pages difficult. Others may benefit from visual supports, tactile elements, or alternative ways of interacting with a text. Without intentional efforts to address these needs, some community members may remain excluded from library services. Before attending the session, my understanding of accessibility largely centered on traditional formats such as large print and braille. Learning about adaptive books expanded that perspective. items.raw_text: I had the distinct honor of attending PLA 2026 in Minneapolis thanks to a PLA scholarship. As an eastern North Dakota native, Minneapolis is a familiar destination, but spending several days surrounded by thousands of energized library professionals made the city feel vibrant and new, despite the wind, cold, snow, and more wind. The connections, reunions, and conversations I experienced throughout the conference reminded me why gatherings like PLA matter. Alongside reconnecting with colleagues and making new professional connections, I left with fresh ideas, practical tools, and renewed optimism about the future of libraries. Several sessions stood out to me, both because of their content and because of the presenters who brought those ideas to life. What impressed me most was how scalable the ideas felt. items.title: Building More Inclusive Libraries for Patrons with Disabilities
items.raw_text: At every conference I attend, I hope to leave with at least one idea I can realistically adapt and implement at my own library. At PLA 2026, I found that inspiration in my very first session: *”Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities.”* Presenter Courtney Walker, founder of Libraries for All, shared how her experience as a school librarian led her to rethink traditional picture book collections for students with disabilities. She noticed that many students were not engaging with standard picture books, often returning them unread or damaged. In some cases, families stopped checking out books altogether. Seeking a solution, Walker adapted a resource commonly used in classrooms: laminated books enhanced with sensory and interactive elements. By modifying these materials for library use and creating durable books with touch-and-feel components, she found that students with disabilities engaged more actively with stories and enjoyed more positive and equitable reading experiences. Walker now works as a consultant through Libraries for All and collaborated with fellow presenters Janet Cox and Maggie Fox of Plano Public Library (PPL) in Texas to develop a full collection of adapted books. Their team selected popular picture books, organized volunteer workshops to create adapted versions, trained staff to support the collection, and developed cataloging practices for these unique materials. items.title: Information Strategies for Libraries in the Age of AI
items.raw_text: Librarians must actively adapt to an information landscape increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence (AI), search engine optimization (SEO), and algorithm-driven content. During the PLA 2026 session, *”Trust & Verify: Information Accuracy in the Age of SEO, AI, and Algorithms,”* Nathaniel Burnard, Systems Services Manager at Allen County Public Library, offered a practical and timely examination of how these forces influence the way we, and our patrons, discover and evaluate information. As a 2026 PLA scholarship recipient, I had the opportunity to attend Burnard’s insightful presentation in Minneapolis. Burnard began by explaining the differences between misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation (MDM). While these terms are often used interchangeably, they differ based on the intent behind the creation or sharing of information. Misinformation is false or inaccurate information shared without intent to deceive. Disinformation is deliberately false information created to manipulate, mislead, or cause harm. Malinformation contains truthful information that is presented in a misleading, sensationalized, or harmful way. To help identify MDM, Burnard encouraged attendees to ask critical questions such as, “Does this content provoke a strong emotional response?” and “Does it use small pieces of valid information that have been exaggerated or distorted?” He also emphasized the importance of avoiding engagement with misleading content.
